desc:
Take an array of distinct integers sorted in ascending order and swap some disjoint pairs of neighbouring elements (no element takes part in more than one swap). The result is nums. So every element is at most one position away from where it would be in the sorted array. Example: [10, 3, 40, 20, 50, 80, 70] is a sorted array with the pairs (10, 3)... no, read it as [3, 10, 20, 40, 50, 70, 80] with the pairs at indices (0,1), (2,3) and (5,6) swapped.

Return the index of target in nums, or -1 if it is not present. Use O(log n) time.
constraints: Every element is at most one position away from its place in the sorted order (disjoint adjacent swaps)
hints: Ordinary binary search compares only nums[mid]. What can go wrong when the element you want sits right next to mid?
The target, if present, can only be at mid - 1, mid or mid + 1 when it belongs 'around' the middle. Check those three cells directly.
If none of the three equals the target, compare the target with nums[mid]: if it is bigger, continue in [mid + 2, hi], otherwise in [lo, mid - 2]. Skipping the checked neighbours is safe.
editorial: An element is at most one cell away from its sorted position, so a sorted-order comparison with nums[mid] is only reliable up to a margin of one cell on each side. The fix is to test mid - 1, mid and mid + 1 for equality at every step, then discard the rest by comparing with nums[mid].

Why the discarding is correct: suppose none of the three cells holds the target and target > nums[mid]. The value at mid has sorted rank at least mid - 1, the target has a larger rank, so its rank is at least mid, and its actual position is within one of that: at least mid - 1. Since mid - 1, mid and mid + 1 are excluded, the target must be at mid + 2 or later. The other direction is symmetric. The window at least halves each time, so the time is O(log n) and the space is O(1).
